newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-RADCLIFFE, VICIOSA WIN FITH AVENUE MILE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-RADCLIFFE, VICIOSA WIN FITH AVENUE MILE.

text.p: Paula Radcliffe of Briatin and Isaac Viciosa of Spain recorded victories in the Fifth Avenue Mile road race on Saturday, after late withdrawals of marquee names took the lustre off both the women's and men's races.

Radcliffe, who easily won her race in a modest 4 minutes, 26.69 seconds, learned the night before that Russia's Svetlana Masterkova, the 1996 Olympic gold medalist at both 800 metres and 1,500 metres, had pulled out because of nausea and flu-like symptoms.

"Without the Olympic champion, it certainly made life easier, though perhaps less challenging," said Radcliffe, who took command of the race shortly after the pacesetter, Jacquline Martin of Spain, dropped out at the half-mile mark.
"Nobody was pushing, so I told myself I wasn't going to run along and wait for the others to move."

The 22-year-old from Loughborough, who won the junior division of the World Cross Country Championships in Boston in 1992, had run mostly 5,000-metre races over the past few years. "For that reason, I was worried about my speed at the end, but it wasn't until the final steps that I could hear anyone behind me."

The steps came from Portugal's Carla Sacramento, who finished second in 4:27.52. Canada's Leah Pells placed third in 4:31.66 followed by Ireland's Sinead Delahunty, the race's defending champion, in 4:31.93. Austria's Therese Kiesl, the Olympic bronze medallist at 1,500 metres this summer, finished eighth and never threatened the leaders.

Viciosa, who won here in 1995, took his first lead in the men's race with 70 metres to go, crossing in 3:53.67 and a step ahead of Morocco's Driss Maazouzi, who finished in 3:54.02. France's Samir Benfares was third in 3:54.33.

Viciosa's countryman Fermin Cacho, the Olympic champion in 1992 and silver medallist this summer, withdrew earlier in the day after complaining of calf pains he suffered while training on Fifth Avenue's cobblestone sidewalk earlier in the week.
The races were held in the streets of the city's well-known thoroughfare, which was closed to traffic.

"I am happy for the second victory here, because I like the atmosphere of New York," said Viciosa. "I knew from running last year that you must be patient because there is a long downhill, which makes the finish seem very close. A road mile is not like the track."
Viciosa said the race was some consolation for a disappointing Olympics in which he was the fastest non-qualifier among the 1,500-metre semi-finalists.
"This is a good way for me to end the season," he said, but no so much for Fermin. I was sorry for him. In New York, you must be careful of everything."
